prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered, top-down layout: the camera wearer’s nearby arms or surrounding people occupy the bright upper region, the hands, tools, and concrete rim are at intermediate depth, and the square opening and ground are farther and darker. Roughly, the working hands and trowel appear about 0.4–0.9 m from the camera, the concrete structure about 0.7–1.3 m away, and the other visible people about 0.8–1.8 m away, but monocular depth does not provide dependable metric scale or distances between people. Across the five frames, the camera shifts rightward around the opening while hands move over the rim; a person entering from the lower edge in frames 4–5 appears farther than the hands but is partly occluded and cut off. The map makes near/far ordering and the recessed opening clearer than RGB alone, but bright clothing merges with near-depth regions, object boundaries are blurred, and fine geometry such as the trowel, fingers, and exact hole depth is unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map supports object-level spatial separation: people are mainly along the upper edge and, in later frames, the lower-right edge, while a long narrow tool lies diagonally near the central work area and the concrete opening itself is mostly unlabeled. The nearest segmented person regions correspond approximately to people within 0.5–1.5 m of the camera, with their hands near the central rim and often within arm’s reach of both the camera wearer and the adjacent worker; exact inter-person distances cannot be recovered from masks alone. Over time, person masks shift from upper-left/upper-center toward upper-right, and an additional partly visible person appears from below in frames 4–5, indicating changing camera position and occlusion rather than a reliable approach measurement. The masks clarify which image regions belong to separate people and expose partial visibility, but labels such as “donut,” “pizza,” and “knife” are visibly unreliable for the mortar container, concrete/ground region, and hand tool, while several people, hands, and construction objects are missed or fragmented.
descriptions.pose: The pose map provides the clearest locations and orientations of visible hands: one hand cluster is near the upper-left work area in frame 1, two overlapping hand skeletons meet near the center in frame 3, one appears right of center in frame 4, and two separated clusters appear near the right side in frame 5. These hands are approximately 0.4–1.0 m from the camera and lie over or beside the concrete rim, placing the tool and work surface within the workers’ arm reach; overlapping skeletons in frame 3 show that two hands are very close to each other, likely within a few tens of centimetres. No dependable body skeletons, heads, or gaze vectors are shown, so the map cannot establish which way whole bodies face or whether anyone looks toward the camera wearer; the RGB only indicates that the upper worker is bent toward the surface. Pose makes finger spread, hand orientation, and hand-to-hand overlap harder to miss than in RGB, but it fails on occluded hands, produces no useful body pose, and may distort finger positions where hands overlap or are partly outside the frame.
